title: 1944 terrain overlays for the slice: hedgerow country and German inundations, June 1944
author: Tov Binyamin Brog

sources.title: G. A. Harrison, Cross-Channel Attack, US Army in World War II, CMH 1951
L. F. Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, HMSO 1962
Martin Blumenson, Breakout and Pursuit, CMH 1961

bocage.name: Cotentin, Bessin and the Bocage
bocage.note: Harrison (pp. 180-181, 284) divides the NEPTUNE area into the north and south Cotentin, the Bessin (hedgerow-enclosed meadows between Isigny and Bayeux), the Bocage (hilly wooded country south of the Bessin and Cotentin nearly to the base of the Brittany peninsula) and the relatively open Caen country from Bayeux east and southeast; he calls hedgerows ubiquitous throughout the Cotentin and the bocage country. Ellis contrasts the open, hedgeless country east of the Orne with the close hedgerows of the bocage. The polygon follows the Caen-country edge Bayeux - Tilly - Villers-Bocage - Thury-Harcourt - Falaise - Argentan - Sees and closes on Alencon - Mayenne - Fougeres - Pontorson. The exact line is Claude's drawing from those descriptions. Blumenson supports the line: the Coutances-St-Lo plateau is typical bocage; the sector east of the Vire is the heart of the bocage country; Montgomery expected the Germans to use the difficult bocage of the Domfront-Argentan-Alencon area; the NEPTUNE planners saw the Allied right sweeping south of the bocage toward Laval-Mayenne and le Mans-Alencon; Brittany meant a change to wide-open exploitation. Brittany and the Pays d'Auge stay outside the polygon.

flood.name: Flooded strip behind Utah Beach
flood.note: Harrison p. 182: a flooded coastal strip about two miles wide from the Bancs du Grand Vey to Quineville, crossed only by causeways. Cells inside the box at or below 6 m are flooded; the 6 m line is Claude's choice.

flood.name: Douve and Merderet inundations
flood.note: Harrison pp. 181-182, 286-287: swamplands of the Douve and its tributaries across about five-sixths of the base of the peninsula; the Germans flooded the Douve and Merderet by partly blocking the lock at la Barquette before D-Day.

flood.name: Lower Aure valley
flood.note: Harrison pp. 181, 367: the Aure between Trevieres and Isigny runs through a broad marshy valley that can be flooded; on D+1 the flats were flooded to a width of half a mile to two miles.

flood.name: Dives valley and delta
flood.note: Ellis: paratroops dropped in flooded ground on either side of the Dives; Rommel proposed withdrawing behind the flooded Dives; inundations made the advance across the Dives delta slow in August.
